step_outcomes.notes: Full scale N=500. (i) After routing S-Inhibition output from pABC into NM queries, NM attention on IO drops 0.584->0.287 and rises on S 0.136->0.302 -- the S-Inhibition heads suppress attention to the repeated (S) name and free NMs to attend to IO, exactly the paper's mechanism. KEY RESULT reproduced: mean-ablating the three main Name Movers changes the logit difference only marginally (3.2645 -> 3.3321, ~ +2%, essentially no drop -- the shipped cell's own comment notes an INCREASE can occur). The direct-effect sweep with NMs ablated then surfaces the Backup Name Mover heads as the new top direct contributors: 10.10, 10.2, 10.6, 10.1, 11.2 -- all members of CIRCUIT['name mover'] beyond the primary three, i.e. the Backup Name Movers -- plus the Negative Name Mover 11.10/10.7 whose effect strengthens. step_outcomes.notes: N=100 (shipped completeness scale). KEY RESULTS reproduced. Faithfulness: full CIRCUIT is faithful (|F(M)-F(C)|=0.399); NAIVE slightly worse (0.574). COMPLETENESS CONTRAST (C19 vs C21): the NAIVE circuit is much MORE INCOMPLETE than the full circuit -- by-class max incompleteness naive=3.007 vs complete=1.342; e.g. removing the name-mover class from NAIVE gives F(C\K)=0.325 while F(M\K)=3.332 (gap 3.007), whereas the full circuit's by-class points stay near the diagonal (max gap 1.342, on 'previous token'). Greedy search yields the LARGEST incompleteness scores (complete 3.443 > random 1.932 > by-class 1.342; naive 3.280 > by-class 3.007 > random 2.685), reproducing the paper's finding that greedy K-selection surfaces incompleteness invisible to by-class removal. NOTE: greedy/random are stochastic (10 runs, seed=0) so exact maxima differ run-to-run; the qualitative ordering greedy>=random and naive-more-incomplete-than-complete is the reproduced claim. All pts/*.pt regenerated fresh (cached tensors NOT used).

All 26 circuit heads have a strictly nonzero minimality score (min 0.0678, max 1.3759) -- reproducing the paper's minimality claim that every circuit node materially contributes (adding v back after removing K measurably shifts the logit difference). The special-cased K sets (name-mover cumulative ordering; (9,0)/(11,9) use name-mover+negative; (5,8)/(5,9) paired with the negative name movers) were reproduced exactly and all asserts (head in its own K set) passed. fixes_applied.description: gen_adv (copied from advex.py) uses show_tokens()->model.to_tokens() to reconstruct token positions, but in this EasyTransformer version to_tokens() PREPENDS a BOS token while the IOIDataset word_idx (prepend_bos=False) does not. The off-by-one broke the punct-position assertion (s[punct_str_idx] not in '.,'). Fixed by tokenizing without BOS via a local toks_list() using model.tokenizer directly, matching how word_idx was computed; this also corrects adv_tok_len (was +1 too large) used to shift end/S2 indices.

step_outcomes.notes: Full scale N=500 (matches plan). KEY RESULT reproduced: the added-IO adversarial attack (a natural distractor sentence that repeats the IO name) collapses model performance -- mean logit diff 3.437 -> 0.593, IO prob 0.494 -> 0.302, and the fraction of examples where the model prefers S over IO jumps from 0.8% (pIOI) to 36.0%. The added-S CONTROL (same kind of distractor sentence but repeating the already-duplicated S name) barely changes performance (logit diff 3.437 -> 3.085, S>IO 0.8% -> 2.2%). This is the paper's adversarial finding: duplicating the IO name triggers the Duplicate-Token/S-Inhibition machinery on the wrong name, whereas adding another S does not, demonstrating the circuit's specific vulnerability.
